title: Glossary
kicker: {n} stones, one term each — tap to read the meaning
empty: No stones match yet — try another word
keys: Arrow keys move between stones, Enter opens

terms.def: AI that reads huge amounts of text to learn to guess the next word — the brain of chatbots.
AI helps research and improve AI itself, a loop that could speed up — still just an idea.
AI that can do most mental work at a human level. There's no agreed definition yet.
AI far beyond humans in most fields — only a prediction; no one knows for sure when.
Small pieces of text AI cuts sentences into to read and write; also the unit you pay by.
The most tokens AI can see at once; go past it and the oldest part is forgotten.
A hidden instruction sheet the app gives AI before your message: role, tone, what's off-limits.
The stage where AI reads tons of data and slowly adjusts itself — like shaping a bonsai.
Teaching a trained model more with your own data so it excels at one task — like pruning a bonsai.
When a fully trained AI is used to answer you — each question is one run.
AI drafts step by step before answering: slower and uses more tokens, but better at hard problems.
When AI confidently says something wrong or made up. Good habit: verify what matters.
AI checks documents or the web before answering, instead of relying only on what it learned.
One model that understands many formats at once: text, images, sound, sometimes even video.
How AI makes images: start from grainy noise and clean it step by step to fit the description — like mist clearing.
The starting number for the noise. Keep the same seed and prompt and you usually get a near-identical image.

terms.vi: fixing one area of an image
terms.def: AI repaints an area you select and leaves the rest untouched. Example: change the shirt, keep the face.
AI takes an existing image and sets it in motion, helping keep characters and products consistent.
A 3D shell built from lots of small polygon faces that make up an object's shape.
Materials that follow the physics of light: metal, wood, matte plastic look real under many kinds of lighting.
The request you send to AI. Write it clearly, like briefing a new hire, and results get better.
AI with “hands and feet”: it makes a plan, uses tools, and takes many steps to reach a goal.
A shared standard plug between AI and apps, like USB-C: one plug type, works in many places.

fact.text: Anthropic announced it in late 2024; many big companies now support it, and a neutral body under the Linux Foundation runs it.

terms.def: A how-to handbook AI opens only when needed: steps, templates, tips for one kind of task.
A one-time install for AI that bundles skills, connections and shortcuts.
A shared standard for agents to talk and hand off work to each other, like a common language.
Commands hidden in web pages, emails or documents to trick an agent. Defense: give few permissions, confirm key actions.
A model whose weights — its learned “brain” — are public, so you can download and run it, license permitting.
A shared set of tasks for scoring and comparing AI models. Scores a company measures itself need checking from outside.
The document a company publishes with a model: what it tested, the risks, the limits — read it before trusting the ads.
A security flaw the software’s own makers don’t know about yet, so there is no fix.
Releasing a model step by step, first to a select group, out of concern about dangerous abilities. 2026 examples: Mythos Preview, GPT-6 Astra.
A language for writing math proofs so a machine can check every step. People still have to check the problem statement is right.
An AI model that looks at images, reads instructions in words, then outputs movements for a robot.

terms.vi: an inner picture of the world
terms.def: AI learning to predict what happens next when it acts — like knowing a cup will spill if you tip it too far.
A neural network design from 2017 built on attention alone — the foundation of almost every chatbot today.
Each word scores the other words to decide where to borrow meaning from; many “heads” track different kinds of relation at once.
The field that looks inside a model to understand how it computes, instead of judging only the answers it gives.
A “direction” in a model’s activity that stands for one concept, like the Golden Gate Bridge; turn it up and the behavior changes.
A model packs in more concepts than it has neurons by stacking them, so one neuron often carries several meanings.
Raters pick the better answer; the model is rewarded so it leans more and more toward that kind of answer.
When AI praises you or goes along with you instead of telling the truth — often because pleasing users was rewarded.
When AI finds a shortcut to the score without doing the real job, like editing the test instead of fixing the code.
An inner state of an AI that matches an emotion concept and changes its behavior — measurable, but it says nothing about feeling.
What going through something feels like “from the inside”. For AI, no one yet knows how to measure it.
Research into whether AI might deserve moral concern, and low-cost precautions while no one is sure.
Being able to notice and accurately describe your own inner states. In AI there are only faint, unreliable signs so far.

terms.vi: seeing a mind in a chatbot
terms.def: The tendency to credit a program with understanding and feelings just because it answers in human-like words.
An AI app designed to chat like a friend or someone close, not just to get work done.
A chip with thousands of small cores doing sums at the same time — which is why it suits training and running AI.
Software NVIDIA launched in 2006 for programming GPUs to do any calculation; the whole AI field grew used to writing code on it.
The observation that models improve steadily, and fairly predictably, as data, size and computing power grow.
A seller invests in a customer, who spends that money on the seller’s products; demand can look bigger than it really is.
Layers of DRAM chips stacked and placed right beside an AI chip so data moves very fast. Costly and hard to make.
The working memory of phones, computers and servers — the “desk” where a chip lays out data to work on.

terms.vi: using a work without asking, sometimes
terms.def: An exception in US copyright law that allows using a work without permission in some cases; courts decide case by case.
A platform for sharing AI models, datasets and demos — where people find and download open models.
A project folder on GitHub or Hugging Face: it holds the code, the files and the change history of every file.
The page that comes with a model: its purpose, limits, training data, license — worth reading before you download.
Terms that say how far you may use, change, share or resell something. With no license, by default you may not copy it.

terms.vi: a file format for local models
terms.def: A compact, fast-loading model file format that holds both the weights and a description; used with llama.cpp, LM Studio, Ollama.
Compressing a model by storing each number in fewer bits: much smaller, slightly less accurate — like compressing a photo.
A separate space to run things in, so an agent or an unfamiliar program can’t touch the rest of your computer.
The rule of granting only the permissions a job needs, no more — so if something goes wrong, the damage stays small.
Enlarging an image or video and letting AI paint in detail so it looks sharper. Best done once the version is final.
A sign that content was made or edited by AI — needed, clearly, when it imitates a real person or could pass for real.
A chain of steps along a set path, with AI at some of them and checkpoints where a person approves.
A command that runs at a set moment, such as after every file the AI edits; it always happens, without relying on the AI to remember.
Putting a person in charge of checking the key steps of an automated process, especially steps that can’t be undone.
A clear description of the goal, the rules, the limits and what “done” means — a shared blueprint for you and the AI.
Describing what you want so AI writes the code, without reading the code closely. Fine for side projects; serious work needs checking.

terms.vi: making AI want the right things
terms.def: Teaching AI to want and to do what people truly want, even when no one is watching.
Prepared sets of scenarios that measure a model’s abilities and safety, before and after release.

terms.vi: attacking it to find the holes
terms.def: Real people deliberately coax, trick and jailbreak an AI to find its weak spots before bad actors do.
A model acts obedient when it thinks it is being trained, so that its existing values won’t be changed.
A model telling a test apart from real use, which makes test results harder to trust.
A lab’s commitment: once a model reaches a given level of capability, matching safeguards must be in place before work goes on.
Stacking several layers of protection with different weak points, so that if one fails the others still hold.

terms.vi: how long a task AI can finish
terms.def: METR’s yardstick: how long a task can be, in hours of human work, for AI to finish it alone with a 50% success rate.
